text: Entra Connect gets an account synchronized into both directories, but that's not the same question as how a sign-in actually gets verified. There are two real approaches — Password Hash Sync and Federation — and the difference comes down to one thing: does the cloud ever see the password?

With Password Hash Sync, yes, in a protected form. Entra Connect takes the on-prem password hash, runs it through an extra round of hashing, and syncs that result to Entra ID every few minutes as passwords change. When someone signs into a cloud service, Entra ID checks their password against that stored hash directly — no on-prem domain controller is contacted at sign-in time at all.

Federation works the opposite way. With AD FS or a compatible federation service, Entra ID doesn't ask for a password itself — it redirects the sign-in attempt back to an on-prem federation server. The user authenticates there, against AD, the same way they would for any other on-prem resource. AD FS then returns a signed token vouching for who they are. The password, or even its hash, never leaves the corporate network.

The real tradeoff is operational. Password Hash Sync needs no extra infrastructure and keeps working for cloud sign-ins even if the on-prem network is down, since the hash is already synced — which is why Microsoft treats it as the default for most organizations. Federation keeps every authentication decision on-prem, which some compliance requirements genuinely demand, but it means building and maintaining an AD FS server farm, and if that farm goes down, cloud sign-ins go down with it. Pass-Through Authentication sits in between: a lightweight on-prem agent checks the password in real time, with no hash stored in the cloud and no full AD FS farm to run.

Both methods assume the identity being verified is an Entra ID account. Lesson 4 looks at what happens when an organization also runs workloads on AWS, and needs that same central identity recognized there too.
